content: Leading health authorities universally recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months postpartum. While many women begin breastfeeding, a significant number discontinue due to challenges they encounter, rather than personal choice. One of the most common difficulties faced by breastfeeding women is painful nipples. Research has identified improper infant positioning or latch as a frequent cause of this issue. Although various interventions have been developed to alleviate nipple pain, it remains unclear which treatment is the most effective. A comprehensive understanding of nipple pain and its treatment options is essential to improve breastfeeding duration and exclusivity rates, as well as to address one of the most common challenges faced by breastfeeding women. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of all interventions aimed at resolving or reducing nipple pain. Additionally, the review sought to assess the impact of these interventions on other outcomes, such as nipple trauma, infections, breast mastitis, breastfeeding duration, exclusivity, and maternal satisfaction. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that evaluated interventions for treating nipple pain in breastfeeding women. Cluster-randomized trials were eligible, but cross-over trials were excluded. The interventions considered included pharmacological treatments (e.g., antifungal creams), non-pharmacological topical treatments (e.g., lanolin), dressings (e.g., hydrogel dressings), nipple protection devices (e.g., breast shells), phototherapy, and the application of expressed breast milk. Women who exclusively fed their infants with expressed breast milk, such as those with infants in neonatal units, were excluded from the review, as their experiences of nipple pain and its treatment differ from those of women breastfeeding directly. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, evaluated methodological quality, and verified data accuracy. Additional information was sought from trial researchers when necessary. Ultimately, four trials of good methodological quality, involving 656 women, were included in the review. These trials evaluated five different interventions: glycerine pads, lanolin with breast shells, lanolin alone, expressed breast milk, and an all-purpose nipple ointment. All studies included education on proper infant positioning at the breast as part of routine postpartum care for both treatment and control groups. Pooled data were available only for the comparison of lanolin versus usual care. Data for other outcomes were not pooled due to heterogeneity in outcome measures or differences in interventions. The findings revealed no significant evidence that glycerine gel dressings or breast shells with lanolin improved nipple pain. One trial found no clear differences in nipple pain between women who applied lanolin and those who applied nothing to their nipples at one to three days, four to five days, or six to seven days post-treatment. However, the same trial reported that women who applied expressed breast milk experienced significantly lower perceptions of nipple pain after four to five days of treatment compared to those who applied lanolin. This beneficial effect, however, was not sustained after six to seven days of treatment. There were no differences in nipple pain perceptions at any time point between women who applied expressed breast milk and those who applied nothing. Women who used an all-purpose nipple ointment, compared to those who used lanolin, did not experience any improvement in nipple pain after seven days of treatment. Overall, there was insufficient evidence to suggest that glycerine gel dressings, lanolin with breast shells, lanolin alone, expressed breast milk, or all-purpose nipple ointment significantly improved maternal perceptions of nipple pain. Importantly, regardless of the treatment used, most women reported that nipple pain reduced to mild levels approximately seven to ten days postpartum. Providing anticipatory guidance about the typical timeline for pain reduction may help women continue breastfeeding and do so exclusively. The overall quality of the evidence for the primary outcome of nipple pain, as assessed using the GRADE approach, was low. This was primarily due to the reliance on single studies with small sample sizes for data analysis. The authors concluded that there was insufficient evidence to recommend any specific intervention for the treatment of nipple pain. The results suggested that applying nothing or expressed breast milk may be equally or more beneficial in the short-term management of nipple pain compared to using ointments such as lanolin. However, the limited number of trials, the variability in interventions, participants, outcome measures, and standards of usual care, as well as the low quality of evidence, precluded robust conclusions.
